m.c: May the God who called Moses and Isaiah give you courage and joy to serve today. Walk with confidence, for his presence goes with you at every step. May his peace and strength accompany you from the morning on. God is taking care of you today.
h: Moses had been a shepherd for forty years in the land of Midian. He had grown up in the palace of Egypt, but now he was tending the sheep of his father-in-law Jethro, far from his people. One day he led the flock to the mountain of God, called Horeb, and there he saw a strange sight: a bush that was burning with fire but was not consumed.

He went over to look, and God called him by name from the midst of the bush: “Moses, Moses!” He answered, “Here I am.” God told him to take off his sandals, for the place where he stood was holy ground. Then he explained that he had seen the affliction of his people in Egypt, that he had heard their cry, and that he had come down to deliver them. And then he said to him: “Now go, I am sending you to Pharaoh, so that you may bring my people out of Egypt.” God did not need Moses to be strong, but to be obedient, and that is why he chose him in spite of his doubts and his years.

Moses made objections. He asked who he was to go before Pharaoh. God did not argue about his smallness; he answered with a promise: “I will be with you.” Moses’ assurance did not rest on his ability, but on God’s company.

Centuries later, the prophet Isaiah lived through a similar scene in the temple. He felt lost before the holiness of the Lord, but a seraph touched his lips with a burning coal and assured him that his sin was forgiven. Then he heard the voice of God: “Whom shall I send?” And Isaiah answered: “Here am I; send me.” In both accounts, God purifies, calls, and accompanies the one who makes himself available. It is a story the people of Israel told for generations: the God who sees, who hears, and who comes down to deliver his own never calls anyone only to abandon them along the way.
m: God still calls today. He does not always do it through a burning bush; sometimes it is through a need that comes your way, through an opportunity to serve, or through a whisper in the heart. The question is whether we are attentive and willing.

First, do not make excuses for your weakness. Moses said he was not eloquent, and God gave him his brother Aaron as a helper. What God asks for is availability, not perfection. If today you feel that you are not up to what has been entrusted to you, remember the promise: “I will be with you.”

Second, let God purify you. Isaiah was first forgiven, then sent. Before you leave to work or to serve, confess to God what weighs on your conscience and receive his forgiveness. A purified heart serves with joy, not with pride or as a burden.

Third, say “here I am” in a practical way. Think of just one person you can serve today: an elderly neighbor, a coworker who is struggling, a relative who is alone. Do it without expecting applause. God uses simple gestures to accomplish great things. As you begin this day, repeat in your heart the words of Isaiah: “Here am I; send me.” And walk with confidence, for the one who calls you goes with you. May this day find you attentive to the voice of God and ready to obey, with the humility of one who knows that power does not come from us.
o: Lord and our God, we thank you for this new day and for the life you lend us. You are holy and at the same time near; you revealed yourself to Moses in a bush that burned without being consumed, and you touched Isaiah’s lips with a coal from the altar. Today we come to you with reverence, knowing that you know us by name and that you do not call us in order to leave us alone.

We acknowledge that, very often, we feel small and inadequate. Like Moses, we ask: who am I? But you answer: I will be with you. Purify our lips and our hearts of everything that gets in the way. Forgive our excuses and our fears. Give us attentive ears to hear your voice in the midst of the noise of the day.

Send us today, Lord, wherever you wish. May we know how to serve at home, at work, and in the street with humility and joy. Give us eyes to see the one who needs help and the courage to reach out a hand. Be yourself our strength when the task seems too great, and remind us that what matters is not so much what we have, but that you go with us. Here we are; use us for your glory. Here we are, Lord, ready to listen to you today. In Jesus’ name, amen.

t.c: Thank you, Lord, for this day in which your grace reached us. Place in his hands whatever was left unfinished and rest in the joy of knowing you are sought and loved. May your home sleep today under his peace. May your night be blessed with true rest.
h: Jesus entered Jericho and was passing through the city. There lived a man named Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector and very rich. Tax collectors gathered taxes for the Roman empire, and people despised them, because many demanded more than was due. Zacchaeus was a powerful man, but surely a very lonely one.

He was trying to see who Jesus was, but he could not because of the crowd, for he was short in stature. So he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see him when he passed by. He had no idea what was about to happen. When Jesus came to that spot, he looked up and said to him: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down; for I must stay at your house today.” Climbing a tree was undignified for an important man, but Zacchaeus did not stop to think about what people would say, because his desire to see the Lord was stronger than his shame.

Zacchaeus came down at once and received him joyfully. The people muttered, because Jesus had gone in to be the guest of a sinner. But Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord: “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone of anything, I will pay back four times as much.”

Jesus answered: “Today salvation has come to this house, because this man, too, is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” The encounter with Jesus changed Zacchaeus from the inside. It was neither the law nor pressure from people that transformed him, but the grace of having been sought and accepted. That day, Zacchaeus went from being a rejected man to a son of Abraham recognized by Jesus in front of everyone.
m: The story of Zacchaeus teaches us that Jesus takes the initiative. While Zacchaeus was climbing the tree out of curiosity, Jesus had already seen him and had his name ready. Tonight you can rest knowing that it is not you who are chasing God in desperation: he is the one who seeks you first.

First, think about what you did today to draw near to Jesus. Perhaps a quick prayer, a reading from the Bible, or an act of kindness. Even if it was small, God saw it. Zacchaeus only climbed a tree, and the Lord stopped.

Second, examine whether there is anything you need to make right. Zacchaeus was not content with the emotion of the encounter; he offered to give to the poor and to repair the wrong he had done. This was not how he bought his salvation, for Jesus had already said that salvation had come to his house. His conduct was the fruit of a changed heart. If you have wronged someone by words or actions, decide to ask forgiveness tomorrow and to repair what you can.

Third, look at others as Jesus looked at them. All around us there are people whom others have pushed aside, like Zacchaeus. Ask God to give you eyes tomorrow to see one of them and the courage to approach. And now, rest. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost, and that includes you. Sleep in joy, for today, too, salvation has come to your house. May your heart be at peace.
o: Lord Jesus, at the end of this day, we thank you because you seek and save the lost. Thank you, because you pass along our road, you look up, and you call us by name. You do not look at us the way the world looks at us, but with a gaze of love that transforms the heart. Praise be to you for your patience with us.

Today, Lord, we want to receive you with joy in our home, as Zacchaeus did. Come into our household, into our thoughts, and into our plans. Show us what we must correct, what we must return, and what we must forgive. Give us an honest heart that does not hide behind the crowd or appearances. Thank you for every opportunity you gave us today to act with justice.

Tonight we place in your hands the worries we could not settle and the people we carry in our hearts. Take care of those who feel alone or rejected, of those whom no one seeks or invites. May they, too, hear your voice saying: today I want to stay at your house. Grant us rest, Lord, and peaceful sleep, for you have had mercy on us. In Jesus’ name, amen. May your grace always reach us, Lord, amen.
